methods.title: Machine learning tasks → clustering versus classification
methods.trigger: A question asks what ML is, which task or learning type a method is, or whether a problem is clustering (no labels) or classification (known labels).

methods.title: Distance between two feature vectors → Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski
methods.trigger: Two points or feature vectors are given and a distance, similarity or dissimilarity between them is needed.

methods.title: k-means clustering → assign to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat
methods.trigger: Unlabeled data, a number of clusters k and initial centroids are given; find labels and new centroids.

methods.title: kmeans() output and the number of clusters → within-cluster sum of squares
methods.trigger: R kmeans() output (size, withinss, tot.withinss, betweenss) is given, or the number of clusters k must be chosen.

methods.title: K-nearest neighbors classification → K smallest distances, plurality class
methods.trigger: A labeled training set and a new object are given; classify the new object or give its class probability using K neighbors.

cases.title: Tomato and its single most similar food
cases.context: A tomato has sweetness 6 and crunchiness 4. It is compared with four labeled foods from the Session 22 food example. Assign it to the class of the one labeled food it is most similar to, using the Euclidean distance.
tasks: Compute the Euclidean distance from the tomato (6, 4) to each of the four labeled foods.
Identify the most similar food and assign the tomato to its class. State whether this is a clustering or a classification problem.

steps.title: Identify the problem type
steps.words: The foods have known classes, so assigning the tomato is a classification problem (supervised).

steps.title: Distance to grape and green bean
steps.words: Subtract matching features, square, add and take the root.

steps.title: Distance to nuts and orange
steps.words: The same formula is applied to every labeled food.

steps.title: Pick the most similar food
steps.words: Orange has the smallest distance, so it is the most similar food. Its class is Fruit, so the tomato is assigned to Fruit.

cases.conclusion: The nearest labeled food is orange at distance 1.41421, so the tomato is classified as a fruit. This uses only one neighbor (K = 1).
cases.source: Original practice example using the Session 22 page 37 food data

cases.title: Three distances between medicines 1 and 4
cases.context: Medicine 1 has features (MW, pH) = (1, 1) and medicine 4 has (5, 4), on the arbitrary scales of the Session 22 medicine example. Compare the Euclidean, Manhattan and Minkowski (p = 3) distances between them.
tasks: Compute the Euclidean and Manhattan distances between medicine 1 and medicine 4.
Compute the Minkowski distance with p = 3 and compare all three values.
cases.symbols: \(q,r\) (two points or feature vectors), \(q_i,r_i\) (their \(i\)th coordinates), \(m\) (number of dimensions), \(p\) (Minkowski order), \(d(q,r)\) (distance).

steps.title: Coordinate differences
steps.words: Find the absolute difference for each feature first, then reuse them in every formula.

steps.title: Euclidean distance
steps.words: Square, add and take the square root.

steps.title: Manhattan distance
steps.words: Add the absolute differences.

steps.title: Minkowski distance, p = 3
steps.words: Cube, add and take the cube root.

steps.title: Compare
steps.words: Larger p puts more weight on the largest single difference, so the distance shrinks toward the largest difference, 4.

cases.conclusion: The Euclidean distance is 5, the Manhattan distance is 7, and the Minkowski distance with p = 3 is 4.49794.
cases.source: Original practice example using the Session 22 page 22 medicine data

cases.title: k-means on ten ages
cases.context: Ten ages are 20, 21, 22, 28, 35, 40, 41, 42, 43 and 44. Cluster them with k-means using k = 2 and initial centroids c1 = 21 and c2 = 30.
tasks: Perform iteration 1: compute both distances for every age, assign labels, and compute the new centroids.
Continue iterating until no label changes. Report the final clusters and centroids.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of entry \(i\)), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(d_{ij}\) (distance from entry \(i\) to centroid \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label of entry \(i\)), \(n_j\) (number of entries in cluster \(j\)), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: In one dimension the Euclidean distance is the absolute difference.

steps.title: Iteration 1 distances
steps.words: Every age gets a distance to both centroids; the full table lists all ten rows.

steps.title: Iteration 1 labels
steps.words: Ages 20, 21 and 22 are closer to 21. Age 28 and above are closer to 30.

steps.title: Iteration 1 centroids
steps.words: Each centroid is the mean of its members.

steps.title: Iteration 2 distances and labels
steps.words: Age 28 is now closer to 21, so it moves to cluster 1. A label changed, so continue.

steps.title: Iteration 2 centroids
steps.words: Recompute both means with the new memberships.

steps.title: Iteration 3 check
steps.words: No label changes, so the centroids stay the same and the algorithm stops.

steps.title: Name the clusters
steps.words: The labels 1 and 2 can be named young and old after clustering.

cases.conclusion: Iteration 1 moves the centroids from 21 and 30 to 21 and 39. Iteration 2 moves age 28 into cluster 1 and gives 22.75 and 40.83333. Iteration 3 changes nothing, so the final clusters are 20–28 and 35–44.

cases.title: k-means on four medicines (MW, pH)
cases.context: Four medicines have features (MW, pH) on arbitrary scales: (1, 1), (2, 1), (4, 3) and (5, 4). Cluster them with k-means using k = 2 and initial centroids c1 = (1, 1) and c2 = (2, 1), with the Euclidean distance.
tasks: Perform iteration 1: compute all eight distances, assign labels, and compute the new centroids.
Perform iteration 2 and report the final labels and centroids.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of entry \(i\)), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(d_{ij}\) (distance from entry \(i\) to centroid \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label of entry \(i\)), \(n_j\) (number of entries in cluster \(j\)), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The initial centroids are medicines 1 and 2.

steps.title: Iteration 1 distances
steps.words: Compute the distance from each medicine to both centroids.

steps.title: Iteration 1 labels
steps.words: Only medicine 1 is closer to c1.

steps.title: Iteration 1 centroids
steps.words: Average each feature over the members of each cluster.

steps.title: Iteration 2 distances and labels
steps.words: Medicine 2 is now closer to c1, so its label changes.

steps.title: Iteration 2 centroids
steps.words: Recompute both centroids with the new memberships.

steps.title: Check convergence
steps.words: A third pass gives the same labels, so the centroids are final.

cases.conclusion: After iteration 1 the centroids are (1, 1) and (3.66667, 2.66667). After iteration 2 the labels are 1, 1, 2, 2 and the centroids are (1.5, 1) and (4.5, 3.5), which do not change on the next pass.

cases.title: Session 22 lecture exercise: SBP and CRP
cases.context: Systolic blood pressure (SBP; mmHg) and C-reactive protein (CRP; mg/L) were measured in 3 adults and standardized, so the scaled values are unitless. Perform a single iteration of k-means with k = 2 and the Euclidean distance, using initial centroids C1 (SBP = 2, CRP = 2) and C2 (SBP = 5, CRP = 5).
tasks: Compute the distance from each patient to C1 and to C2, showing the intermediate calculations.
Give the cluster label of each patient and the new centroids of the two clusters after this single iteration.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of entry \(i\)), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(d_{ij}\) (distance from entry \(i\) to centroid \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label of entry \(i\)), \(n_j\) (number of entries in cluster \(j\)), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Distances for patient 1
steps.words: Patient 1 is (1, 3).

steps.title: Distances for patient 2
steps.words: Patient 2 is (7, 2).

steps.title: Distances for patient 3
steps.words: Patient 3 is (8, 7).

steps.title: Assign labels
steps.words: Each patient goes to the centroid with the smaller distance.

steps.title: New centroids
steps.words: Cluster 1 has only patient 1, so its centroid is that patient. Cluster 2 averages patients 2 and 3.

cases.conclusion: The labels are patient 1 → cluster 1, patients 2 and 3 → cluster 2. After one iteration the new centroids are C1 = (1, 3) and C2 = (7.5, 4.5).

cases.title: Within-cluster sums of squares for the ages
cases.context: The ten ages 20, 21, 22, 28, 35, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44 are clustered by kmeans(age, c(21, 30)) in R. The final clusters are 20, 21, 22, 28 (centroid 22.75) and 35, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44 (centroid 40.83333). Reproduce withinss, tot.withinss and betweenss, and use the R results for k = 3 and k = 4 to choose k.
tasks: Compute SS for each of the two clusters and tot.withinss for k = 2. Find betweenss from the total sum of squares.
Using tot.withinss for k = 1 to 4, choose the number of clusters.
cases.symbols: \(SS_j\) (within-cluster sum of squares of cluster \(j\)), \(x_i\) (entry value), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Cluster 1 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 1 centroid and add.

steps.title: Cluster 2 sum of squares
steps.words: Use the unrounded centroid 245/6 to avoid rounding drift.

steps.title: Total within-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: This is tot.withinss in the R output.

steps.title: Between-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: R reports this as betweenss, 784.8167. At k = 1 the whole total is within-cluster.

steps.title: Compare k = 1 to 4
steps.words: The drop from k = 1 to k = 2 is about 785; later drops are about 53 and 24.5.

steps.title: Choose k
steps.words: Beyond k = 2 there is only modest improvement, so two clusters are chosen.

cases.conclusion: withinss is 38.75 and 50.83333, tot.withinss is 89.58333, and betweenss is 784.81667. Since tot.withinss improves only modestly for k > 2, k = 2 is chosen.

cases.title: Classifying the tomato with K = 3
cases.context: A tomato has sweetness 6 and crunchiness 4. Classify it with K-NN using K = 3 and the Euclidean distance to four labeled foods from the training set.
tasks: Compute the distance from the tomato to each food and identify the K = 3 nearest neighbors.
Classify the tomato and give the probability that it is a fruit.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: The slide rounds these to 2.2, 4.2, 3.6 and 1.4.

steps.title: Rank and keep K = 3
steps.words: The three nearest neighbors are orange, grape and nuts.

steps.title: Count classes
steps.words: Two neighbors are fruits and one is a protein.

steps.title: Classify
steps.words: Fruit is the most common class among the three neighbors.

cases.conclusion: The three nearest neighbors are orange, grape (fruits) and nuts (protein), so the tomato is classified as a fruit with probability 2/3.

cases.title: Quality control of surgical mesh with K = 3
cases.context: Surgical mesh from four vendors was tested for strength (x1, kg/m²) and flexibility (x2, integer scale 1–10) and graded Pass or Fail by surgeons. A new vendor's mesh has x1 = 7 and x2 = 3. Classify it with K-NN using K = 3 and the Euclidean distance.
tasks: Compute the distance from the new mesh (7, 3) to each vendor, rank them, and identify the K = 3 nearest neighbors.
Classify the new mesh as Pass or Fail and give the probability that it fails.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The training set has four labeled vendors.

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: Compute the distance to every vendor.

steps.title: Rank the distances
steps.words: Ranks are C 1, D 2, A 3, B 4, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are C, D and A.

steps.title: Read the neighbor classes
steps.words: Vendor B is not a neighbor, so its class is not used.

steps.title: Classify and give the probability
steps.words: Fail is the plurality class, so the new mesh is classified as Fail.

cases.conclusion: The three nearest neighbors are C (Fail), D (Fail) and A (Pass). The new mesh is classified as Fail, with probability 2/3 of failing the surgeons' assessment.

sampleQuestions.stem: For the tomato (6, 4) compared with grape, green bean, nuts and orange, what is the Euclidean distance to its single most similar food?
sampleQuestions.why: Orange (7, 3) is closest: \(\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2\approx1.41421\). Adding the differences without squaring gives 2, which is the Manhattan distance.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the Euclidean distance between medicine 1 (1, 1) and medicine 4 (5, 4)?
sampleQuestions.why: The differences are 4 and 3, so \(\sqrt{16+9}=5\). 25 forgets the square root, and 7 is the Manhattan distance.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the Manhattan distance between medicine 1 (1, 1) and medicine 4 (5, 4)?
sampleQuestions.why: Manhattan adds absolute differences: \(4+3=7\). Subtracting them gives 1 and multiplying gives 12.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the Minkowski distance with \(p=3\) between medicine 1 (1, 1) and medicine 4 (5, 4)?
sampleQuestions.why: Cube the differences, add, and take the cube root: \(91^{1/3}\approx4.49794\). 91 skips the root and 30.33333 divides instead of taking a root.

sampleQuestions.stem: In iteration 1 of the ages example (\(c_1=21\), \(c_2=30\)), what is the distance from age 28 to \(c_2\)?
sampleQuestions.why: In one dimension the distance is \(|28-30|=2\). 7 is the distance to \(c_1\), and 4 squares the difference.

sampleQuestions.stem: After iteration 1 of the ages example, what is the new centroid of cluster 2?
sampleQuestions.why: Cluster 2 holds 28, 35, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, so \(273/7=39\). 40.83333 is the iteration 2 centroid, and 45.5 divides by 6 instead of 7.

sampleQuestions.stem: After iteration 2 of the ages example, what is the centroid of cluster 1?
sampleQuestions.why: Age 28 joins cluster 1 in iteration 2, so \(c_1=(20+21+22+28)/4=22.75\). 21 is the old centroid and 30.33333 divides by 3.

sampleQuestions.stem: After iteration 2 of the ages example, what is the centroid of cluster 2?
sampleQuestions.why: Cluster 2 is 35, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, so \(245/6=40.83333\). Dividing by 7 keeps the old count and gives 35, and 41 is one member value, not the mean.
